title: Inventory policy under uncertain demand
description: An offline mathematical-simulation template, not a target-program execution. Replace its claim, assumptions, scenarios, design points, and outcomes with a mathematical representation of the user's system before treating it as evidence.

designPoints.description: Challenge point where added stock may have little practical benefit.

outcomes.name: fill_rate
outcomes.description: Share of simulated demand fulfilled from available stock.

outcomes.name: unmet_units
outcomes.description: Simulated demand that could not be fulfilled.

hypotheses.claim: The higher-stock policy improves mean fill rate by at least 0.05 relative to baseline across the declared demand range.
hypotheses.estimand: paired mean difference in fill_rate (higher-stock minus baseline-stock)
hypotheses.decisionRule: Use Hoeffding-Bonferroni intervals with at least 95% simultaneous coverage over this hypothesis's design points, conditional on independent replication pairs and valid a priori arm bounds. Support if every lower endpoint is at least 0.05; challenge if any upper endpoint is below 0.05; otherwise report inconclusive. The small demonstration budget may be insufficient for a decision.
hypotheses.falsificationRule: Use the low-demand challenge point to test whether added stock no longer clears the 0.05 improvement threshold.

assumptions.statement: Period demand is represented by max(0, Gaussian(mean, sd)), a clipped draw with a point mass at zero, independently across replications at each design point.
Unmet demand is lost and stock does not carry between periods.

For nonnegative stock and demand, fulfilled demand is between zero and demand; define fill rate as one for zero demand. Both policies therefore have fill rate in [0, 1] for every possible draw, not just for observed draws.

variableReview.scope: Compare single-period fulfillment at assumed demand settings. This does not establish the economically best operating policy. Adapt this inventory to the new problem; do not preserve inventory-specific candidates mechanically.

variables.label: Available starting stock
variables.mechanism: Fulfilled demand is min(stock, realized demand); adding stock helps only when demand exceeds the original stock.
variables.evidence: Assumed policy levels; a3-fill-rate-support supplies the accounting bound.
variables.reason: This is the intervention, not an independent random demand draw.
variables.nextCheck: With demand fixed at 110, compare stock 100 and 115; verify fulfilled demand and both outcomes by hand.

variables.label: Demand distribution location
variables.mechanism: Changes the Gaussian location before clipping at zero. It is not exactly the mean of realized clipped demand.
variables.evidence: Assumed typical and low-demand settings, not calibrated measurements.
variables.reason: Different demand regimes may change whether extra stock clears the practical threshold.
variables.nextCheck: Set demand_sd to zero and vary demand_mean across the stock threshold; verify the expected piecewise response.

variables.label: Demand distribution spread
variables.mechanism: Changes variability before clipping and the mass above the stock threshold.
variables.evidence: Assumed dispersion; the two demonstration design points change location and spread jointly.
variables.reason: Variability changes shortages; the present grid cannot isolate its marginal effect from location.
variables.nextCheck: Use a fresh crossed location-by-spread design for sensitivity; include the zero-spread boundary.

variables.label: Demand shape and tail behavior
variables.mechanism: a1-demand-shape fixes max(0, Gaussian(location, spread)), including a point mass at zero.
variables.evidence: Illustrative assumption, not evidence that real demand follows this family.
variables.reason: The template demonstrates one mechanism; it does not compare distribution families.
variables.nextCheck: In a fresh mathematical model, compare a skewed or mixture demand family at comparable realized moments.

variables.label: Fulfilled demand and outcome accounting
variables.mechanism: Derive fulfilled=min(stock,demand), unmet=demand-fulfilled and fill_rate=fulfilled/demand; define fill_rate=1 when demand=0.
variables.evidence: Model identities and a3-fill-rate-support, not a separately sampled input.
variables.reason: Keeping the accounting derived prevents impossible independent combinations or double counting.
variables.nextCheck: Verify conservation, zero demand, zero stock, and fill_rate in [0,1] for all tested draws.

variables.label: Stock carry-over and backlogged demand
variables.mechanism: Inventory and unmet demand can affect later periods; the single-period model has no such state transition.
variables.evidence: a2-single-period excludes both mechanisms by scope, not by measured insignificance.
variables.reason: The current estimand is single-period fulfillment, not a multi-period operating policy.
variables.nextCheck: Ask whether unmet demand is lost or backlogged and whether inventory persists; if needed build a separate multi-period simulation.

variables.label: Demand persistence, seasonality and customer mix
variables.mechanism: Correlated demand or heterogeneous customers can change aggregate risk and the applicability of independent-period results.
variables.evidence: No time series or subgroup evidence supplied; independence is an assumption.
variables.reason: The demonstration has independent replications, no calendar and no customer-level state.
variables.nextCheck: Inspect existing evidence for regimes and dependence; use assumed regimes in a fresh simulator if decision-relevant.

variables.label: Starting-stock availability constraint
variables.mechanism: Delayed or capped supply can make the declared starting-stock policy infeasible.
variables.evidence: No existing supply constraints supplied; both stock levels are assumed available.
variables.reason: Policy feasibility is not established by a conditional fulfillment comparison.
variables.nextCheck: Ask whether both stock levels can be supplied; test bounded availability or lead-time scenarios mathematically.

variables.label: Holding, shortage and purchase costs; budget
variables.mechanism: Higher fulfillment may not justify its cost; economic utility is absent from the declared outcomes.
variables.evidence: No prices or objective weights supplied; no economic-optimality claim is identified.
variables.reason: This candidate affects the broader decision even though it does not alter the present accounting outcomes.
variables.nextCheck: Ask which costs, budgets and service constraints define a better policy; add outcomes and assumptions in a fresh economic model.

interactions.mechanism: The min operation makes the stock benefit depend jointly on demand location and spread, with a saturation region.
interactions.reason: Separate one-factor averages can miss the region where added stock stops helping.
interactions.nextCheck: Check below, at and above stock thresholds, then cross location and spread in a fresh sensitivity design.

interactions.mechanism: The fixed demand family and dispersion jointly determine tail mass above available stock.
interactions.reason: The mechanism is present but robustness across demand families is not tested.
interactions.nextCheck: Compare rival mathematical tail mechanisms without asserting that this template has already tested them.

interactions.mechanism: Persistent demand and remaining inventory can jointly amplify future shortages.
interactions.reason: There are no multiple periods or feedback states in this model.
interactions.nextCheck: For a multi-period decision, compare an explicit state-transition model under plausible persistence and backlog assumptions.

coverageChecks.note: Trace both outcomes through fulfillment to the three implemented parameters; inspect the economic objective separately.
Consider supply, starting stock, demand fulfillment, then remaining stock or unmet demand. Only the middle single-period stage is modeled.
Location and spread vary jointly in the demo; feedback and temporal dependence remain omitted.
No customer segments or selected demand history are represented; one family need not generalize to a mixture.
Do not extrapolate independent single periods into a validated long-horizon capacity policy.
Check conservation and support bounds; distinguish a mathematically defined stock level from feasible supply or budget.
Skewed demand and a multi-period backlog mechanism are untested alternatives, not additional replication noise.
Inputs are assumptions. Missing evidence must remain visible; it does not authorize executing the real system.

openQuestions: Is the decision strictly about single-period service, or must it include cost, feasibility and future periods?
Which existing evidence bounds demand regimes, supply availability and the cost of a shortage?
What omitted mechanism would most plausibly reverse your preference between the two policies?

uncertaintyContract.systemVariability: Independent max(0, Gaussian(mean, sd)) demand draws conditional on each design point; an illustrative clipped-demand assumption, not a universal demand model.
uncertaintyContract.simulationError: Conservative finite-sample uncertainty for the paired mean contrast under fixed-count independent pairs and a priori arm support; the empirical MCSE is separate from the Hoeffding interval width.
uncertaintyContract.parameterUncertainty: Separate explicit demand design points; no probability weights are inferred from this grid.
uncertaintyContract.structuralUncertainty: Demand shape, temporal dependence, and carry-over mechanisms remain assumptions to challenge in an adapted study.
uncertaintyContract.predictiveScope: Replication-level demand fulfillment, not a measured production forecast. Add a separate validated analysis for predictive quantiles or tail risk when requested.
